content: Supplementary oxygen is commonly administered to low-risk pregnant women undergoing elective caesarean sections under regional anaesthesia. However, the effects of this practice on maternal and neonatal outcomes remain unclear. This review updates a previous analysis first published in 2013. The primary aim of the review was to assess whether providing supplementary oxygen to low-risk term pregnant women during elective caesarean sections under regional anaesthesia could prevent maternal and neonatal desaturation. A secondary aim was to compare maternal and neonatal blood gas levels between women who received supplementary oxygen and those who did not. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering literature up to November 2014. The search was updated in February 2016, identifying one additional study awaiting classification for future review updates. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving low-risk pregnant women undergoing elective caesarean sections under regional anaesthesia were included, comparing outcomes with and without oxygen supplementation. Data extraction and quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses were also performed. The updated review included 11 trials with a total of 753 participants. The evidence was of low quality and showed no significant differences in Apgar scores at one minute (based on six trials with 519 participants) or at five minutes (also based on six trials with 519 participants). None of the included trials reported cases of maternal desaturation. Very low-quality evidence indicated that women receiving supplementary oxygen had higher maternal oxygen saturation, maternal arterial oxygen pressure (PaO2), foetal umbilical arterial oxygen pressure (UaPO2), and foetal umbilical venous oxygen pressure (UvPO2) compared to those breathing room air. These findings were based on three trials (209 participants) for maternal oxygen saturation, six trials (241 participants) for maternal PaO2, eight trials (504 participants) for UaPO2, and ten trials (683 participants) for UvPO2. However, there was significant heterogeneity among these outcomes. Subgroup analysis revealed no significant difference in UaPO2 between intervention groups in low-risk studies, but high-risk studies showed a benefit for the neonatal oxygen group. In conclusion, the review found no strong evidence to suggest that administering supplementary oxygen to healthy term pregnant women during elective caesarean sections under regional anaesthesia is either beneficial or harmful in terms of short-term clinical outcomes, as measured by Apgar scores. While higher maternal and neonatal blood gas values were observed with supplementary oxygen, these results should be interpreted cautiously due to the low quality of the evidence.
